Where does collagen go after you drink it? Collagen supplements don't travel intact from your stomach straight to your skin or joints. Your digestive system breaks collagen down into smaller components, including amino acids and peptides, which are then absorbed and used by the body. Collagen is particularly rich in amino acids such as glycine and proline, which are among the building blocks involved in protein and collagen production. Vitamin C also plays an important role in normal collagen formation. Research has also explored whether certain collagen peptides may have signaling effects, so the story isn't simply “collagen gets destroyed.” The bigger takeaway? You're supplying raw materials, not shipping finished collagen directly to your skin. 💬 What benefit are you hoping to get from collagen? #collagen #collagenpeptides #collagenpowder #vitaminc #glycine #proline #protein #aminoacids #skinhealth #jointhealth #supplements #nutritiontok

Collagen is what gives skin its structure, firmness, and bounce. And while we naturally make less of it as we age, there are ways to support what we have and encourage new production: - Vitamin C: An essential cofactor your body actually needs to synthesize and stabilize collagen. - Sun protection: UV exposure activates enzymes that break down collagen and contributes to photoaging. Protecting your skin helps preserve the collagen you already have. - Collagen generators: I use BioSil, a stabilized form of orthosilicic acid (ch-OSA). Human studies suggest it can support the body’s own collagen production and improve measures of skin elasticity and texture. - Red light therapy: Specific wavelengths of red/NIR light can influence cellular signaling and fibroblast activity, with studies showing improvements in collagen density and skin appearance. Wavelength and dose matter, which is why I prioritize quality devices. - Adequate protein: Collagen is a protein. Your body needs amino acids, especially glycine, proline  and lysine, as the raw materials to build it. Collagen supplements are a perfect example of where the marketing can sound much more convincing than the evidence. The idea is appealing: take collagen every day, give your body the building blocks it needs, and expect firmer, more hydrated skin in return. But when you look closely at the research, the picture is much less clear-cut. Some studies do report modest improvements in things like hydration and elasticity after regular use, but the evidence is mixed, study quality varies, and a lot of the positive data comes from industry-funded research. That doesn’t mean collagen supplements are completely useless. It does mean I’d be cautious about treating them as an essential anti-ageing investment. If your budget is limited, I’d put the basics first: daily SPF, a well-formulated retinoid if appropriate, good skincare, adequate protein and nutrition, and treatments with a stronger evidence base if you want to go further. Spend where the evidence is strongest, not where the marketing is loudest. If you want more straight-talking skincare and ageing advice, follow along 💬
